lessons.title: Compile First, Run Later
lessons.objective: Explain when Rust catches errors compared with Python, and what rustc produces.
lessons.hook: Most Rust bugs you hit will be compiler messages, not crashes, so you need to expect them.
lessons.aside: Rust compiles ahead of time. CPython also compiles to bytecode, but it checks almost no types before running.
lessons.explain: Python checks most errors only when the faulty line executes, so a type mistake in a rarely used branch can hide for weeks. Rust works differently. rustc compiles Rust source into a native executable before it runs. Type and borrow errors are reported at compile time, so the program never runs with them. Example: `let x: i32 = "hi";` is rejected with a mismatched-types error. No binary is produced and nothing executes. In Rust, fighting the compiler takes the place of hunting runtime exceptions.
key_facts: rustc compiles Rust source into a native executable before it runs.
Type and borrow errors are reported at compile time, so the program never runs with them.
Python checks most errors only when the faulty line executes.
fixes: Expects Rust errors to appear at runtime like Python exceptions.

predict.q: A Rust file has a type error inside a function that main never calls. What happens when you build it?

It builds with only a warning

angles: Think of a publisher's editor who reads the whole manuscript before printing. Python is more like a reader who discovers typos page by page. Which of the two would stop a bad page from ever reaching readers?
An airport security check happens before boarding, not mid-flight. Map that idea onto when Rust looks at your code compared with Python.
claims: rustc produces native executables.
Rust reports type errors at compile time.
A Rust program with a type error produces no binary.
Python reports most errors only when the faulty line executes.

misconceptions: Rust checks lines as they execute like Python

options: It is checked only when that line runs

items.answer: It is checked only when that line runs
items.why: Python raises most errors when the faulty line executes.
misconceptions: Python has a compile step that hides warnings
Errors inside functions are silently skipped

misconceptions: Rust executes line by line until it hits a fault

items.q: In one sentence, when does Rust report type errors compared with Python?
items.answer: Rust reports them at compile time, before the program runs, while Python reports most errors only when the faulty line executes.
accept: Rust reports them before running; Python reports them during running
Rust catches them at compile time
items.why: Rust's checks happen before any code executes.

items.q: What tool turns Rust source into an executable?
items.why: rustc compiles Rust source into a native executable.

lessons.title: Cargo: New, Run, Release
lessons.objective: Create, run and release-build a Rust project with cargo.
lessons.hook: Cargo fills the roles of pip, venv and a build tool in a single command.
lessons.aside: Dependencies go under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml, roughly like a requirements file.
lessons.explain: `cargo new name` creates a project with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Inside it, `cargo run` compiles the project and then runs the binary. For production, `cargo build --release` builds an optimized binary in target/release. The generated main.rs prints with `println!("Hello, world!");`. `println!` is a macro, and the `!` marks a macro call; it is not an ordinary function. Example: `cargo new greet && cd greet && cargo run` prints Hello, world!
key_facts: `cargo new name` creates a project with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs.
`cargo run` compiles the project and then runs the binary.
`cargo build --release` builds an optimized binary in target/release.
`println!` is a macro; the `!` marks a macro call.

Run `cargo ___ calc` to create the project. `cd calc`, then `cargo ___` to compile and run it. For an optimized binary, run `cargo build ___`, which writes to target/___.

lessons.title: let, mut and Shadowing
lessons.objective: Declare immutable and mutable variables and use shadowing correctly.
lessons.hook: Your first Rust compile error is likely to be reassigning a variable.
lessons.aside: Shadowing is common when parsing input, for example turning a string into a number while reusing the same name.
lessons.explain: In Python, any name can be reassigned. In Rust, `let` bindings are immutable by default, and assigning twice to a non-mut binding is a compile error. `let mut` makes a binding mutable. Example: `let count = 1; count = 2;` fails, but `let mut count = 1; count = 2;` compiles. Shadowing with a new `let` creates a new binding with the same name, as in `let x = 5; let x = x + 1;`. The old x is not mutated. A new x replaces it from that line on.
key_facts: `let` bindings are immutable by default.
`let mut` makes a binding mutable.
Assigning twice to a non-mut binding is a compile error.
Shadowing with a new `let` creates a new binding with the same name.
fixes: Assumes variables can be reassigned freely as in Python.
angles: A Rust binding is like a value written in pen on a label unless you ask for a pencil when you create it. Which keyword asks for the pencil?
Writing a fresh label and sticking it over an old one is different from erasing the old one. Decide which of these describes writing `let` again.
claims: let bindings are immutable by default.
let mut allows reassignment.
Reassigning a non-mut binding is a compile error.
Shadowing creates a new binding.

items.q: By default, a `let` binding is:
items.why: Rust bindings are immutable unless marked mut.
misconceptions: Rust names behave like Python names
let wraps values in a refcount

items.q: `let total = 0; total = 10;` gives:
items.why: A non-mut binding cannot be assigned twice.
misconceptions: reassignment is free as in Python
the error is caught at runtime

items.q: How do you allow `score` to be reassigned?
items.why: mut comes right after let.

items.q: `let x = 5; let x = x * 2;` What is this?
items.why: A second let creates a new x.
misconceptions: shadowing changes the old value in place
the second x points at the first

items.q: What keyword makes a variable reassignable?
items.why: let mut makes a binding mutable.

items.q: What happens if you assign twice to a binding declared with plain `let`?
items.answer: The compiler rejects it with a compile error.
items.why: Assigning twice to a non-mut binding is a compile error.

lessons.title: Static Types and Inference
lessons.objective: Read and write basic type annotations and predict inferred types.
lessons.hook: Types are how the compiler catches bugs before your program ever runs.
lessons.explain: In Python, a name can hold an int and later a str. In Rust, every Rust value has one type fixed at compile time. The compiler infers most types, so annotations are often optional: `let n = 7;` needs none. Integer literals default to i32 and float literals to f64. Example: `let a = 7;` is i32, `let b = 2.5;` is f64, and `let c: u8 = 200;` is explicitly an unsigned 8-bit integer. Writing `let a = 7; let s: String = a;` fails because an i32 is not a String.
key_facts: Every Rust value has one type fixed at compile time.
The compiler infers most types, so annotations are often optional.
Integer literals default to i32 and float literals to f64.
angles: Picture a filing cabinet where each drawer is stamped for one kind of document. The stamp can be read off the first document you file. Which part of that picture is inference?
Python type hints are suggestions that Python itself does not enforce at runtime. Imagine hints that the build refuses to ignore. What changes about when mistakes surface?
claims: Rust types are fixed at compile time.
Rust infers most types.
Integer literals default to i32.
Float literals default to f64.

items.q: What is the default type of `let k = 42;`?
items.why: Unannotated integer literals default to i32.

items.q: Can a variable hold an i32 and then a String?
items.why: Each value's type is fixed at compile time.

items.q: Why does `let n = 7;` compile without an annotation?
items.why: Inference makes most annotations optional.
misconceptions: Rust has a dynamic any default

items.q: `let r = 1.5;` has what type?
items.why: Float literals default to f64.
misconceptions: C type names apply in Rust

items.q: What are the default types for integer and float literals?
items.answer: i32 for integers and f64 for floats.
items.why: These are Rust's literal defaults.

items.q: When is a Rust value's type fixed?
items.why: Every Rust value has one type fixed at compile time.

lessons.title: Ownership: One Owner, Dropped at Scope End
lessons.objective: State the ownership rules and say when a value is freed.
lessons.hook: Ownership is how Rust frees memory without a garbage collector.
lessons.aside: CPython frees most objects by reference counting. Rust works out the freeing point at compile time instead.
lessons.explain: Each value in Rust has exactly one owner, the variable responsible for it. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped, which means its memory is freed. A scope is the block between curly braces where a binding is valid. Example: `{ let s = String::from("hi"); }`. Inside the braces s owns the text. At the closing brace s goes out of scope and the String is dropped automatically. There is no `del` and no garbage collector pass.
key_facts: Each value in Rust has exactly one owner.
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.
A scope is the block between curly braces where a binding is valid.
angles: A library book is checked out to exactly one card at a time, and it goes back to the shelf automatically when that card expires. Map the card, the book and the expiry onto Rust terms.
Picture a hotel room key that is valid only until checkout. Which part of a Rust program plays the role of the stay?
claims: Each Rust value has exactly one owner.
Values are dropped when their owner leaves scope.
Scopes are delimited by curly braces.

items.q: How many owners can a Rust value have at once?
items.why: Ownership is unique.
misconceptions: owners are like Python names sharing an object

items.q: When is a String owned by `s` freed?
options: When s goes out of scope
items.answer: When s goes out of scope
items.why: The value is dropped at the end of its owner's scope.

items.q: What marks a scope in Rust?
items.why: A block between braces is a scope.

items.q: `{ let t = String::from("x"); } // here` What is true at `here`?
items.why: The closing brace ends t's scope.

items.q: State the two ownership rules covered in this lesson.
items.answer: Each value has exactly one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped.
accept: one owner; dropped at end of scope
items.why: These are the core ownership rules.

items.q: What happens to a value when its owner goes out of scope?
items.answer: It is dropped, which frees its memory.
items.why: Leaving scope triggers a drop.

lessons.title: Moves: Assignment Transfers Ownership
lessons.objective: Predict when a String is moved and why the old name becomes unusable.
lessons.hook: Your guess about moves was right. This lesson shows why, so you can rely on it.
lessons.explain: In Python, `b = a` makes two names share one object. In Rust, assigning a String to another variable moves ownership: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a;` makes b the only owner. After a move, using the original variable is a compile error (E0382, use of moved value), so `println!("{a}")` fails to compile. This rule guarantees the String is freed exactly once. Passing a String to a function also moves it. After `consume(b)`, b cannot be used either.
key_facts: Assigning a String to another variable moves ownership.
After a move, using the original variable is a compile error.
Passing a String to a function also moves it.
fixes: Assumes `let b = a;` makes both names share one value like Python.

predict.q: `let a = String::from("x"); let b = a; println!("{a}");` Result?

angles: Handing someone your only house key is different from cutting them a copy. After the handover, what can you no longer do?
Python's own docs say assignment binds a name to an object without copying it. Rust adds one rule on top: only one name may own that object. Work out what that means for the first name.

Using a moved-from variable is error E0382.
Passing a String to a function moves it.

items.why: A moved-from variable cannot be used.
misconceptions: assignment shares data as in Python

items.answer: To free the String exactly once
items.why: A single owner means a single drop.
misconceptions: the rule is about speed only

items.q: What is the compile error you get for using a moved value? Give the code or the phrase.
items.why: E0382 reports use after move.

items.q: In Python, `b = a` shares one object. What does `let b = a;` do with a String in Rust?
items.answer: It moves ownership to b, and a can no longer be used.
items.why: Rust assignment of a String moves ownership.

lessons.title: Clone and Copy
lessons.objective: Decide when a value is copied, moved or must be cloned.
lessons.hook: Knowing which types copy automatically explains why `let y = x;` sometimes leaves x usable.
lessons.explain: `.clone()` makes an explicit deep copy, so both variables own separate data. Example: `let b = a.clone();` leaves a and b both usable, each with its own String. Types that implement Copy, like i32, bool, and char, are copied instead of moved, so `let y = x;` with an i32 keeps x valid. String is not Copy because it owns heap memory. Copying it silently would hide an expensive allocation, so Rust makes you write clone. This differs from Python's `copy.deepcopy`, which you call only when you want it.
key_facts: `.clone()` makes an explicit deep copy, so both variables own separate data.
Types that implement Copy, like i32, bool, and char, are copied instead of moved.
String is not Copy because it owns heap memory.

predict.q: `let x = 5; let y = x; println!("{x}");` Result?

i32, bool and char implement Copy.
String does not implement Copy because it owns heap data.

items.q: After `let b = a.clone();` with a String a:
items.why: clone creates separate owned data.

items.q: Which type is Copy?
items.why: Simple scalar types are Copy.

items.q: Why isn't String Copy?
items.why: Heap-owning types must be cloned explicitly.

items.q: `let f = true; let g = f;` Is f still usable?
items.why: bool is copied, not moved.

items.answer: For example i32 and bool (char also works).
items.why: These implement Copy.

lessons.title: References: Borrowing Without Owning
lessons.objective: Pass values by shared and mutable reference so the caller keeps ownership.
lessons.hook: Borrowing lets functions use your data without taking it away.
lessons.explain: `&x` creates a shared reference that borrows x without taking ownership. A function taking `&String` can read the value and the caller keeps ownership. Example: `fn len(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }` called as `len(&name)` leaves name usable afterward. Unlike a Python name, a shared reference cannot mutate the value. To change it you need `&mut`. `&mut x` creates a mutable reference, and requires x to be declared `mut`. For example, `let mut v = vec![1]; add(&mut v);` lets add push to v.
key_facts: `&x` creates a shared reference that borrows x without taking ownership.
A function taking `&String` can read the value and the caller keeps ownership.
`&mut x` creates a mutable reference, and requires x to be declared `mut`.
fixes: Expects a shared reference to allow mutation, as Python shared names do.
angles: Lending a friend a book to read is different from lending them the book and a pen to annotate it. Ownership stays with you either way. Which lending needs extra permission?
A museum visitor may look at a painting, but only a restorer with special permission may touch it. Match each role to a kind of Rust reference.
claims: &x creates a shared reference without taking ownership.
Shared references are read-only.
&mut x requires x to be declared mut.

items.why: & borrows without ownership.

items.q: What must a variable be declared as before you can take `&mut` of it?
items.why: &mut x requires x to be declared mut.

items.q: Why can the caller still use name after calling `len(&name)`?
items.answer: Because &name only borrows it, so ownership stays with the caller.
items.why: Shared references don't take ownership.

lessons.title: The Borrow Checker's Rules
lessons.objective: Predict which combinations of references the borrow checker accepts.
lessons.hook: These rules rule out data races and dangling pointers at compile time.
lessons.aside: These are the same guarantees that make sharing data across threads with Send and Sync safe later on.
lessons.explain: At any time you may have either any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference. The borrow checker enforces these rules at compile time. Example: `let r1 = &s; let r2 = &s;` is fine, but `let r = &s; let m = &mut s; println!("{r}");` fails, because r is still used while m exists. A borrow lasts until its last use, not necessarily to the end of the scope. Drop the final println and it compiles. Also, a reference must never outlive the value it points to, so returning `&` to a local is rejected.
key_facts: At any time you may have either any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference.
The borrow checker enforces these rules at compile time.
A borrow lasts until its last use, not necessarily to the end of the scope.
A reference must never outlive the value it points to.
fixes: Has no model of a borrow checker; expects aliasing plus mutation to be allowed.

predict.q: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s; a.push('x');` Result?

A reservation ends when you leave the table, not when the restaurant closes. Use that to reason about how long a borrow lasts.
claims: Rust allows many shared references or one mutable reference at a time.
The borrow checker runs at compile time.
Borrows end at their last use (non-lexical lifetimes).
References cannot outlive their referent.

items.why: This is the core aliasing rule.

items.q: How long does a borrow last?
items.answer: Until its last use, not necessarily to the end of the scope.
items.why: Borrows end at their last use.

lessons.title: Reading and Fixing Borrow Errors
lessons.objective: Diagnose an E0502 error and fix it by reordering code or cloning.
lessons.hook: Reading compiler errors well is the most useful practical skill in day-to-day Rust.
lessons.explain: Read the error code and the labeled spans: where the borrow starts, where the conflict is, where the borrow is used later. Example: `let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!("{first}");` gives E0502, because v is borrowed as shared by first and then mutably by push. Fix a shared-vs-mutable conflict by ending the shared borrow's last use before the mutation, so move the println above push. If you need an independent value, clone it instead of holding a reference: `let first = v[0].clone();`. `rustc --explain E0502` prints a long explanation of an error code.
key_facts: Read the error code and the labeled spans: where the borrow starts, where the conflict is, where the borrow is used later.
Fix a shared-vs-mutable conflict by ending the shared borrow's last use before the mutation.
If you need an independent value, clone it instead of holding a reference.
`rustc --explain E0502` prints a long explanation of an error code.

predict.q: `let f = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!("{f}");` What does the compiler say?

angles: A crime-scene report names where it started, where the conflict happened and where the evidence was seen again. Treat each label in the error as one of those clues. Which clue tells you what to move?
If two people need the same note and one wants to scribble on it, you can either finish reading first or make your own copy. Decide which fix fits each of the two options.

rungs.text: Error E0502 on `let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!("{first}");`. Spans: the shared borrow at &v[0], the mutable borrow at push, and the later use at println. Fix: move `println!("{first}");` above `v.push(4);` so the shared borrow ends first. Alternatively, write `let first = v[0].clone();`.

`let name = &names[0]; names.clear(); println!("{name}");` The error code is E____. The shared borrow starts at ____, the conflict is at ____, and the later use is at ____. Fix: move the ____ before clear(), or replace the reference with `names[0].____()`.
`let top = &stack[stack.len()-1]; stack.pop(); println!("{top}");` Name the error, label the three spans, and give two different fixes.

claims: E0502 means a value cannot be borrowed as mutable while it is also borrowed as immutable.
Ending a borrow's last use before mutation fixes the conflict.
Cloning avoids holding a reference.
